claims.text: ``explicit`` is deliberately not touched here. structcore has no branch context, so its edge set contains the dead-branch and swallowed-import edges ``_split_imports`` withheld two blocks up; merging them back turned every one of those refusals into a silent ``reachable``.
claims.why: The claim refers to '_split_imports' and 'structcore' which are outside this chunk; the code here does not modify 'explicit', which is consistent, but cannot verify the reason about structcore.

claims.text: PER-TIER visited set, deliberately not the global ``claim``. Sharing them stopped a tier's walk dead at any module some other entry had already claimed -- ``spine/picker.py`` carries a __main__ guard, so it was claimed at depth 0 and the ``cli:improve`` walk never got through it to attempt.py or worktree.py, which then degraded to the coarsest attribution available. Traversal must cross claimed nodes; only the first tier to ARRIVE writes the claim.
claims.why: The code implements a per-tier visited set (line 886) and uses claim.setdefault to only write the first arrival (line 896). The example about spine/picker.py is not verifiable from this chunk, but the mechanism is as described.

claims.text: (owner, text) pairs of every string literal a NON-test module carries, plus agent/persona JSON.
claims.why: The function _literal_corpus collects from non-test modules (line 961) and agent JSON files (line 963).

claims.text: A test naming a module proves the test imports it, not that anything dispatches to it -- counting test literals here would launder an island into ``unknown`` and hide exactly what we are looking for.
claims.why: The function explicitly skips test modules (line 961), consistent with the claim.

claims.text: Owners are kept (rather than one concatenated blob) for two reasons: a module's own docstring must not be evidence for itself, and "who names it" is the only part of this signal a human can act on.
claims.why: The function returns a list of (owner, text) tuples, preserving ownership. The code does not self-evidence because _evidence excludes the module's own literals (line 984).

claims.text: Matching is on the DOTTED name or the path, never on a bare stem: "core" or "status" appears in prose everywhere, and a stem match would mark half the tree ``unknown`` -- a report that says "I don't know" about everything is as useless as one that lies.
claims.why: The probes list (line 982) includes dotted and rel, but does not include the bare stem; stem is only used to check __init__ (line 981).

claims.text: A module's OWN literals are excluded: this file's docstring names this file, and self-evidence would make every module that documents itself permanently unknowable.
claims.why: In _evidence, line 984 checks if owner == rel and skips if so.

claims.text: ``entry`` is the strongest claim in this report -- "a human types this and it runs". It is therefore the one claim that gets verified rather than believed: the module must exist AND define the named function.
claims.why: The code checks that the module exists in known_rels (line 1015) and that the attribute is in src.toplevel (line 1021).

claims.text: A dead target (`pkg = "pkg.cli:nosuchfunc"`) raises the moment anyone runs it, and granting it ``entry`` would paint the whole closure behind it green on the strength of a line in packaging metadata that nothing executes.
claims.why: The code adds to broken list when module not found (line 1018) or attribute not found (line 1022), not to entries.

observations.what: The tiered BFS uses a per-tier visited set, but the frontier list is sorted each iteration; this may affect performance but correctness remains.
The _discover_entries function is incomplete in this chunk; it defines add and func_targets locals and processes console scripts, but the rest of the function is missing.

The classification logic for 'unknown' modules uses 'weak' and 'ev' evidence; if weak is non-empty, the reason becomes about dead branches, overriding any literal evidence. This is intentional per the comment.

The 'island' classification includes a note about test coverage, but the condition for 'orphan' is checked before 'island', so modules that import nothing and are not imported become 'orphan', not 'island'.
